newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO aim to clear Hebron hurdles on Monday.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO aim to clear Hebron hurdles on Monday.

text.p: Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said Israeli and Palestinian negotiators were aiming to remove all obstacles to an elusive deal on the West Bank town of Hebron by late on Monday.

"We hope that by tomorrow evening we'll find solutions to the subjects that remain in dispute," he told reporters on Monday after a 90-minute meeting with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in the self-ruled Gaza Strip.

Mordechai said negotiators would iron out the last disputes so that by Monday evening Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could set a time to sign the deal giving Palestinians control of 80 percent of Hebron.
Officials say the signing could take place by Tuesday, the end of the year, and a redeployment in the town within hours.

"I hope that the new year, 1997, will be the year of solving all of the unsolved problems," Arafat told their joint news conference at the Palestinian police station where their late-night meeting took place.
"We hope the meeting between me and His Excellency, the prime minister, will be very soon," Arafat said.
Hebron is the last of seven occupied West Bank cities Israel agreed to give self-rule to under an agreement signed with the PLO in 1995. The PLO took over much of the Gaza Strip in 1994.
U.S. President Bill Clinton's Middle East envoy Dennis Ross was due back in the region on Monday to mediate any last-minute snags and attend the signing.

Security concerns have held up the handover in Hebron, including demands by Netanyahu for additional measures he says are needed to protect the 400 Jewish settlers in the heart of the town of 100,000 Arabs.

"I hope that we'll fight together against terrorism, prevent bloodshed and find a way to advance the process," Mordechai said. Islamic suicide bombings that killed 59 people in Israel in February and March initially delayed the handover.
Under the 1995 accord, Hebron was due to have been given self-rule nine months ago.
Underscoring the tensions in the town, military sources said petrol bombs were thrown at Israeli army targets on Sunday but no one was hurt and no damage was done.

Arafat said the sides had yet to resolve a question of Palestinian participation in patrols near the Tomb of the Biblical Patriarch Abraham, known to Moslems as al-Ibrahimi mosque. The tomb is due to remain under Israeli control.
Arafat also said he still hoped they would agree on Israel's release of more Palestinian prisoners the day of the signing.

The right-wing Netanyahu, who ousted Prime Minister Shimon Peres in May on a promise of better Israeli security, reminded the world on Sunday that a Hebron deal did not mean Jews would leave the town.
"Anyone who tells you we are leaving Hebron is telling you a lie. We're there and we're there forever. The Jewish people are not leaving Hebron," he told U.S. students on Sunday.

In Cairo, foreign ministers from Egypt, Syria and six Gulf Arab states asked the United States, as a broker of Middle East peace, to put financial pressure on Israel to stop settling Jews in occupied Arab lands.
Some 130,000 Jews live in the West Bank and Gaza Strip in settlements scattered among two million Palestinians.
